item.title: ‘Maxxing’ is just self-care and improvement repackaged for social media
item.description: Constantly focusing on how to maximise ourselves may inadvertently cause us to become more focused on what is wrong with us.
item.content:encoded:
If you want to improve yourself, your health or your lifestyle, you need to do it to the “maxx” – according to social media, at least.

If you want to better your appearance, you need to try “looksmaxxing”. If you want to fix your diet and look after your gut, you should be “fibremaxxing”. And if you want to improve your social skills and be more charming, you really ought to be “personality-maxxing”.

But all of this maxxing might not actually be a good way to motivate yourself into healthier habits. In fact, it may have the opposite effect – and may even cause stress.

The language of “maxxing” has roots in the gaming concept of “min-maxing”, in which players strategically maximise desirable attributes while minimising less useful ones to create the most effective in-game character. The concept then made it’s way to the mainstream, most notably through “looksmaxxing”: making focused, and sometimes extreme, efforts to maximise physical attractiveness.

The suffix has since been adapted in multiple health and wellbeing spaces. If there is an aspect of life that could be improved, it can probably be maxxed.

item.title: Kolkata: Protesters paint ‘Anandabazar Patrika’ office saffron after row over headline

The protest came days after the newspaper used the phrase “saffron hooliganism” in a headline about the August 20 clash between student groups at Jadavpur University.

The newspaper’s authorities repainted the walls to their original colour a few hours later.

The men who painted parts of the building have not yet been identified, and no complaint has been filed yet, The Hindu reported.

item.title: Hyderabad: SIR deletions equal 89% of 2023 Assembly election turnout, shows study
item.description: Muslims made up 40.7% of deletions, Sabar Institute said, adding that it could not state if they were deleted at higher rate due to lack of religion-wise data.
item.content:encoded:
The number of voters removed from Hyderabad’s draft electoral rolls during the special intensive revision – 19.4 lakh – was equivalent to 89% of the votes polled in the city in the 2023 Assembly elections, according to analysis done by a Kolkata-based research organisation.

There were 42 lakh voters on the list in January 2023, The News Minute reported.

In two Assembly constituencies – Malakpet and Yakutpura – the number of electors deleted was higher than the number of votes polled in the seats in 2023, Sabar Institute said in its report.

The deletions were equivalent to 112% of the votes polled in Malakpet and 110% in Yakutpura. Both constituencies are represented by the All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen and recorded the lowest voter turnout in Hyderabad district in the 2023 elections, The News Minute reported.

In all 15 Assembly constituencies in Hyderabad, the number of electors deleted was higher than the winning margin in the 2023 Assembly elections, the Sabar Institute said.

Muslims account for 40% of all deletions

Muslims accounted for 40.7% of all deletions, the institute said. However, the report could not determine whether Muslim voters were deleted at a higher rate than other voters because religion-wise elector data at the constituency level is not available, it said.

item.title: How a male Marathi theatre star defined the role of the perfect Hindu wife in the 20th century
item.description: Bal Gandharva’s star persona became a site where respectable Hindu femininity was produced and commodified.
item.content:encoded:
For much of the 20th century, the most admired wife in Marathi-speaking India was not a woman at all.

Bal Gandharva (1888–1967), a celebrated impersonator of Marathi sangeet natak (musical theatre), played devoted heroines with such conviction that film actresses well into the 1970s were trained to reproduce his mannerisms.

How did a man come to define middle-class femininity with such authority?

My recently published research traces Gandharva’s enactment of womanhood from the stage to the marketplace.

It reveals how his star persona became a site where respectable Hindu femininity was produced and commodified – a project that the theatre industry, emerging consumer culture and Hindu nationalist politics each exploited for their own ends.

Staging respectability

India’s pervasive caste system divides Hindus into distinct groups based on which caste they are born into, with certain castes regarded as “higher” than others.

Some of these “lower” castes are made up of hereditary performers: families with a lineage of performing arts. Historically, women from these communities were allowed – and sometimes expected – to perform and entertain.

But Marathi sangeet natak, which emerged in the mid-19th century, was a predominantly upper-caste and middle-class practice.

item.title: China, US and India should compensate Nepal for climate change, says Kathmandu days after floods
item.description: As the toll in the flash floods climbed above 1,000, Foreign Minister Shisir Kanal said that the country was paying for a crisis it did not create.
item.content:encoded:
China, the United States and India, the top industrial emitters of carbon dioxide, have a “historical responsibility to compensate” Nepal as it deals with the consequences of climate change, the country’s Foreign Affairs Minister Shisir Khanal was quoted as saying by The Kathmandu Post on Tuesday.

The statement came five days after a flash flood in the Rasuwa district along Nepal’s northern border with China, which has killed 1,003 persons. Of these, 987 deaths were reported in Nepal. The remaining 16 deaths were on the Chinese side of the border. Nearly 4,500 persons are missing, reported AFP.

The United States Geological Survey has said that the floods were caused by a glacial collapse that sent a wall of water and debris downstream. As there was no rainfall in the area, residents did not have a warning about the deluge.

In an interview to Kantipur TV, Khanal described the disaster as a “catastrophic mountain tsunami”, which he said was a direct consequence of global climate change, reported The Kathmandu Post.

“Nepal’s greenhouse gas emissions are virtually negligible,” the minister was quoted as saying. “Yet, we are paying the ultimate price for a global crisis we did not create.”

item.title: Jet fuel prices for domestic airlines hiked by over 5%, commercial LPG rates up by Rs 10
item.description: This was the second consecutive monthly increase in the price of aviation turbine fuel, taking the rate to Rs 121.2 per litre from Rs 115.
item.content:encoded:
The jet fuel prices for domestic airlines were increased by Rs 6.2 per litre on Tuesday, a hike of more than 5%, NDTV Profit quoted unidentified sources at Indian Oil Corporation Limited as saying.

This is the second consecutive monthly increase in the price of aviation turbine fuel, which now stands at Rs 121.2 per litre.

On August 1, the rate was raised to Rs 115 per litre from Rs 110. In July, it had been reduced by Rs 5 per litre.

The latest increase will add to the financial burden on airlines, as aviation turbine fuel accounts for about 40% of their operating expenses.

The war in West Asia has pushed up global oil prices and led to airspace restrictions that have increased operating costs.

On April 26, Air India, IndiGo and SpiceJet told the Union government that the country’s aviation sector was on the verge of “stopping operations” and had sought its intervention “for immediate and meaningful financial support to tide over the current situation”.

Air India said on May 13 that it would temporarily suspend its services on certain international routes from June to August due to airspace restrictions over some regions and record-high prices of jet fuel.

item.title: New NCLT bench stays order clearing Subhash Chandra’s Rs 6.2 crore repayment plan
item.description: The media baron has admitted claims of about Rs 22,006 crore in his personal insolvency resolution process.
item.content:encoded:
A five-member bench of the National Company Law Tribunal on Tuesday stayed the approval of a repayment plan under which media baron Subhash Chandra was allowed to pay Rs 6.2 crore to creditors against admitted claims of about Rs 22,006 crore in his personal insolvency resolution process, reported Bar and Bench.

On August 25, National Company Law Tribunal Member (Judicial) Nilesh Sharma approved the repayment plan that would have translated into a haircut of approximately 99.9%.

The tribunal is a quasi-judicial body that deals with corporate insolvency and company-law disputes.

In finance, when a creditor is owed a certain amount of money but the debtor only repays a portion of it, the percentage of the write-off is known as a “haircut”.

Since 2022, Chandra has been the subject of insolvency proceedings filed by Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited, now known as Sammaan Capital.

Chandra had stood as a personal guarantor for a Rs 170 crore loan given to a firm, Vivek Infracon. After the loan turned bad, Indiabulls moved the National Company Law Tribunal in 2022 under Section 95 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code for insolvency proceedings against Chandra. The pledge, announced Monday by Hindus for Human Rights Action and SACRED Acts, commits elected officials and candidates across eight American states to reject contributions connected to the RSS and its affiliates. The signatories include members of Congress, state legislators, mayors, local elected officials and candidates from both Democratic and Republican circles.

The six-page pledge also asks politicians to reject political violence and intimidation; and return money from RSS entities and supporters or redirect it to organisations supporting democracy.

Among the most prominent signatories are members of the US House of Representatives Pramila Jayapal of Washington, Ro Khanna of California and Robin Kelly of Illinois. item.title: This book on news photography in India examines how some images became the nation’s visual memory
item.description: An excerpt from ‘All in a Flash: News Photography in India’, by Binoo K John.
item.content:encoded:
When the Covid pandemic hit around March 2020, death itself lost its meaning because everyone was dying or was on the waiting list to hell. The wail of the ambulance, too, had lost its meaning because that sound had become the only noise in that deadly silence that had descended on the world. In Delhi, there was no space to bury the mounting dead. There was no farewell unless you treated the honking of the ambulance as a dirge or the drumbeats that herald Yama, the god of death. Bodies were being dumped all over. For a news photographer, it could be heaven or hell. How do you capture the inevitability of people dying in front of you? Hospitals were no longer a place to go to recover and live. You went there to die. The transition was uncomplainingly smooth. There were no goodbyes. You were bundled in half-alive and stretched out fully dead. The next stop was the pavement outside the overflowing crematoriums.

item.title: August hottest since 1901, September rainfall likely below normal: IMD
item.description: The El Niño conditions that hamper rains are expected to strengthen further in the coming months, said the India Meteorological Department.
item.content:encoded:
Last month was the hottest August since 1901, the India Meteorological Department said on Monday. It also forecast that the rainfall in September will be below normal.

The average temperature across the country was 28.01 degrees Celsius, warmer than the normal of 27.34 degrees Celsius during the month.

The average maximum temperature during the month was 31.66 degrees Celsius instead of the normal of 31.01 degrees Celsius, the weather department said. The average minimum temperature was 24.36 degrees Celsius, higher than the normal of 23.6 degrees Celsius.

In eastern, northeastern and southern India, the average maximum temperature was more than 1.1 degrees Celsius higher than the normal.

September forecast

The weather department also said that the southwest monsoon rainfall in most part of the country will be below normal and less than 91% of the long period average.

The long period average is the measure of the mean rainfall during the four-month monsoon season over the last 50 years.

However, some areas in the northwest, northeast, east, east-central and southeast peninsular India, are likely to receive normal to above-normal rainfall, it said.

The average maximum temperatures are likely to be above-normal in most parts of the country, the India Meteorological Department said.

item.title: When an Indian politician pushed for an anti-communist alliance of Asian democracies
item.description: As India seeks closer cooperation with the US and Asian partners against China, Minoo Masani’s thought is relevant to New Delhi’s strategic posturing.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump’s tenure has vindicated many in the Indian foreign policy establishment prone to reflexive anti-Americanism. However, the recent history of intensified engagement between India and the US, the ongoing bureaucratic collaboration, and the Indian ruling establishment’s cautious reaction to Trump suggest New Delhi’s receptivity to a turnaround in the relationship.

India’s continued insistence on better ties with the US provides an opportune segue to analyse the historical roots of the pro-American, liberal ideational strand of Indian internationalist thought.

Against the backdrop of the Cold War geopolitics, this particular vision offered an alternative to former Indian Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru’s non-aligned, zone of peace approach to the Asian regional security order. Nobody represented the Indian liberal internationalist vision as forcefully as Minoo Masani, the founding leader of the Swatantra party (1959-74).

Based on previously unused archival sources, this inquiry into Masani’s vision for India’s place in the Asian security order highlights a crucial strand of Indian internationalism during the early Cold War years, motivated by a strong sense of both geopolitical and ideological assault by the communist movement.

Lentils, beans and chickpeas have been feeding people for thousands of years. Lentils are among the world’s earliest cultivated crops, with archaeological evidence tracing them back to the beginnings of agriculture. Yet scientists are still learning what happens inside our bodies when we eat them.

A 2026 review of the research examined the evidence on pulses and their effects on the gut and metabolism. Pulses are the dried edible seeds of legume plants, including lentils, chickpeas, dried beans and dried peas. Legumes are the wider plant family and also include foods such as soya and fresh peas.

The researchers brought together evidence from human studies with laboratory and animal research. So what does the science suggest pulses actually do once we eat them?

1. They feed microbes in your gut

Pulses provide plant protein and fibre, along with carbohydrates that are not always completely broken down before they reach the large intestine.

There, gut microbes get involved. When some bacteria break down fibre and other carbohydrates, they produce substances called short-chain fatty acids. These help support the lining of the gut and are involved in how the immune system and metabolism work.

Thus Far

Gather all the footprints you’ve left thus far
on earth – be it in cafés, in cities, on bridges,
farthest continents, across the tidal dance
of a fable, beneath the felling gaze of a lover,
or within the duplicitous denials of dirt. Gather
them in a bag of jute, tied with a string of reed,
and release them into the ravening sea. Gather
all the footprints you’ve left thus far on earth
– they won’t fall, as dust, or be whisked
away, like mist. They’ll swirl, at first, then
tread the contours of a letter, before framing
their sorrows and their memories and their
triumphs and their longitudes through
the creation of a solitary word – Gati –
the Buddhist name for Destiny.

I think of half-eaten goodbyes,

item.title: ‘Fake claims’: Great Nicobar lighthouse project study lists species found in Africa, Amazon
item.description: More than 90% of the species in the tables in the environmental impact assessment study for the Indira Point plan have never been reported from Great Nicobar.
item.content:encoded:
Species primarily found in Africa and the Amazon have been listed in a recent environment impact assessment study claiming that they live on Great Nicobar Island.

The report released in April was prepared by WAPCOS Limited, a Gurgaon-based public sector undertaking as part of a proposal to repair the lighthouse and construct tourist facilities at Indira Point, the southern-most point of the island – and of India.

Tables in the environment impact assessment report list tiger fish (Hydrocynus vittatus), a native of African freshwater rivers, and the flagtail (Semaprochilodus insignis), an Amazonian freshwater fish.

Also listed are sambar (Cervus unicolor) and barking deer (Muntiacus muntjak), two species of mammals found primarily on India’s mainland.

More than 90% of the species listed in the tables in the study have never been reported from Great Nicobar. In many cases the closest sites are thousands of kilometres away.

Ecologists and marine biologists who have spent decades studying Great Nicobar said the report was “shocking” and alleged that it was “completely fabricated”.

The study includes the Eurasian woodcock (Scolopax rusticola), a bird of temperate and subarctic Eurasia that is found in Sri Lanka and along India’s western coast only in the non-breeding season, and the Mayabandar rice frog (Microhyla chakrapanii), which has only ever been reported from the Andaman Islands but not the Nicobar.

item.title: Microfinance promised economic freedom but created more debt for the poor
item.description: It was aimed at low-income households in Asian countries, including India, typically excluded from traditional banking.
item.content:encoded:
Microfinance was once celebrated as Asia’s tool to lift people out of poverty. From Bangladesh to India, Cambodia and the Philippines, the promise was simple: provide small loans to low-income households, help them start businesses, increase income and escape poverty.

Pioneered in the 1970s, microfinance was designed to provide financial services to low income people typically excluded from traditional banking.

Small loans, usually between US$200 and US$500 (about Rs 19,000- Rs 47,000 at current exchange rates) were particularly targeted at empowering women to start businesses and support their families. According to the World Bank, more than 1.7 billion people do not have access to banking.

Yet decades of experience suggest that credit alone has not delivered the transformation to economic independence promised.

We need to ask a difficult question: what if we solved the wrong problem?

Based on flawed assumptions

One fundamental problem is the assumption that poor households in developing nations lack capital but have profitable investment opportunities.

In reality, many poor families operate very small businesses such as food stalls, small shops, farming, tailoring or petty trading. These activities are often labour intensive and face intense local competition.

item.title: Amrita Pritam’s two Delhis: The city she lived in and the city she wrote
item.description: The writer was born on August 31, 1919, in Gujranwala, Punjab Province. She came to Delhi in 1947.

I have spent the better part of a decade reading and rereading Amrita Pritam in Punjabi, Hindi, and Urdu. Every once in a while, I translate her into English, as a way of staying close to her. Beyond the poem written on a train during Partition, the marriage she left, the half-smoked cigarettes of half-requited love, the 40 unwed years spent flouting mid-century convention, I have come to find two Delhis: the city she lived in and the city she wrote.

Pritam arrived in Delhi in 1947 and remained there until she died in it in 2005. She had a working relationship with the city – an announcer’s job, a daily commute, a house paid for, in effect, by 33 years of editorial labour – and a separate, far less forgiving relationship with it as a subject. An old black cat slept snugly in its chair in the Yunnan-themed, street-facing restaurant on Mae Salong’s main road. It was oblivious to the gentle exhortations of two middle-aged women, who asked it to make way for three hungry travellers, excited about the halal fare served there. Beneath a picture of the Kaaba, photos of tantalising soups, noodles, and salads were hung.

The food was not quite Thai, not quite Burmese, certainly Yunnan-inspired, yet very familiar to the three of us. The neighbouring shop played Chinese pop music, and the signs around us were written in English, Thai and Chinese. On the street outside the restaurant, two bystanders spoke in accented Thai, telling us the cat was not going to move, so we ought to find another table.

We had driven two hours from Chiang Dao in northern Thailand in search of tea, supposedly the Assamica variety, grown in the region since the 1980s. My Thai-Australian friends had been here before and they remembered the road being rougher than the smooth, tarred highway we were on.

I, on the other hand, kept marvelling at the landscape, which reminded me of Northeast India. “We could be driving anywhere between Nagaland and upper Assam, you know,” I repeated.

His pen name itself means ‘garden’ in Urdu. But his Punjabi heritage survives in numerous ways. In fact, his early writings and film credits mention his name as ‘Gulzar Deenvi’, a tribute to his birthplace.

The recipient of the Gyanpith Award and the Sahitya Akademi fellowship, among other accolades, displays a rich Punjabi flavour in his writings. item.title: Cottage cheese: Do the protein claims add up?
item.description: There is relatively little research on the impact that cottage cheese has on muscle gain and weight loss.
item.content:encoded:
Cottage cheese is having a moment. It’s being added to dips, mixed into batters and even used in pizza and brownies. It’s touted as a high-protein food that can help build muscle and lose fat. But the research supporting these benefits is not quite as abundant as the number of viral cottage cheese recipes that are out there.

My colleagues and I published a review last year which provided a full breakdown of the available evidence.

Interestingly, our review did not identify any published studies which directly examined the effects of cottage cheese on muscle mass, growth and function. There were also no studies investigating whether eating cottage cheese leads to meaningful changes in body weight or body composition.

This means that much of the current hype around cottage cheese and its benefits is really only based on what we know about protein in general. There is actually relatively little research on the impact that cottage cheese has on muscle gain and weight loss.

The United States of America turned 250 this year amidst political upheaval, economic anxiety, and declining trust in institutions. This has left many Americans questioning the meaning of national-level experiments. At such a moment, I pondered over the writings of John Steinbeck, which felt surprisingly contemporary. More than half a century after his death, the author’s works still reflect upon the moral choices that confront the nation today.

In the words of his biographer, Jay Parini, “Steinbeck is one of the great writer-didacts, which means he was a perpetual student of humanity’s ways and means. item.title: ‘The Struggle’: This impactful novel in translation presents a lived experience of agrarian unrest
item.description: Showkat Ali’s novel gets its emotional and narrative depth from how personal struggle is woven into the wider socio-political fabric.
item.content:encoded:
There’s an intensity to Bangladeshi writer Showkat Ali’s novel The Struggle (translated from the Bengali by V Ramaswamy and Mohiuddin Jahangir) that stayed with me well after I had finished it. Set in rural Bengal in the 1940s, the story doesn’t have any dramatic twists; instead, it builds through accumulations of hardship, small indignities, fleeting kindnesses, and most importantly, the will to endure. The result is a novel that feels both real and historically grounded without becoming didactic.

This story is about Phulmoti, a young widow navigating a world that is structured to box her in from all sides. Widowhood is not just a personal loss; it becomes a social condition that strips her of protection and rights and exposes her to scrutiny and exploitation. Her relationship with Qutubali, an unexpected ally, is one of the novel’s best parts. The novel as a whole resists easy sentimentality; what emerges is something more fragile and believable, shaped by circumstance rather than idealism.

item.title: Kuchipudi has lost its theatrical soul. An 85-year-old guru is trying to bring it back
item.description: In Kuchipudi’s birthplace, Master Rattiah is passing on an old tradition that asks dancers to sing, recite poetry, deliver dialogue and inhabit characters.
item.content:encoded:
Master Rattiah reserves his sharpest rebuke for dance that chooses spectacle over rigour. “Decoration,” he said, with scathing contempt. At 85, he has earned the right to be exacting. Pasumarthi Rattiah Sarma – Master Rattiah to generations of dancers – is among the few remaining masters of the nearly extinct Yakshagana form of Kuchipudi that is a complex alloy of theatre, dance, music and poetics.

For Rattiah, Kuchipudi is not merely movement: the dancer must sing, recite poetry, deliver dialogue and inhabit a character. The form he learnt as a young man demanded all of this, as well as the stamina for punishing footwork and the control to make all that effort invisible.

“I want controlled energy like a spring, not force,” he said. “The face and body should at all times show lalityam (grace), no matter how much effort you put in. Remember that the landscape of Kuchipudi dance is never flat.”

This month, in recognition of his mastery, Rattiah was awarded the fellowship of the Sangeet Natak Akademi. It is an acknowledgement of a tradition that has changed dramatically in his lifetime. item.title: The contradiction in diplomat KM Panikkar’s vision of a maritime strategy for India
item.description: He called on accepting an alliance with a great power patron to secure its neighborhood, a policy that is at odds with India’s ‘strategic autonomy’.
item.content:encoded:
Over a decade has passed since India sought to reorient its grand strategic discourse from continental to maritime Asia and anchored its vision of international order in the Indian Ocean Region.

In justifying this maritime turn within India’s national security discourse, both internal architects and external observers have pointed to the enduring strategic vision of Kavalam Madhava Panikkar (1895-1963). Panikkar was a historian, diplomat and influential foreign policy personality in pre- and post-independence India.

He served in different capacities at princely courts in the erstwhile British Raj, was part of deliberations over India’s geostrategic position during the interwar years, and had crucial stints as independent India’s ambassador to China and then Egypt. Panikkar’s influence was wide-ranging, but in contemporary foreign policy circles, one of his key legacies is the role he played in defining the contours of India’s maritime strategy.

Panikkar’s naval thought, laid out specifically in India and the Indian Ocean: An Essay on the Influence of Sea Power (1945), is consistently invoked to defend both the legitimacy of the grand strategic narrative embedded in New Delhi’s more recent maritime turn, and the convergence of partner states’ Indo-Pacific strategies seen through a “Mahanian” veneer. Queer love has a way of dismantling inherited ways of life with inhabited feelings of desire that compel every person – queer or not yet – to introspect their own trysts with romance, with an enforcement of honesty. Homo and Juliet, written by Shruti Chakravarty, is one such book of eight real-life love stories of lesbian couples and non-binary persons. item.title: Dimagi Naxals? The sages of the Vedas and the Upanishads would qualify today

The highway between Lagos and Ibadan was built in 1978 at the height of Nigeria’s oil boom. Lagos is the country’s largest city, with an estimated population of over 20 million, and Ibadan the third-largest and home to a globally renowned university.

But the boom years are over and rising traffic and decades of neglect have turned the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway into one of Nigeria’s deadliest motorways, earning it the nickname “highway of death”.

Yet even as the 127km stretch of road has faltered as a transport corridor linking north and south, it has flourished as a stage for public religion. Today, lined with sprawling prayer camps, it’s also known as the “spiritual highway”. Religious billboards have replaced road signs and religious camps have been established along the route.

For years my research as an anthropologist has explored how multi-faith settings challenge conventional ideas of religion. Attracting tens of thousands of worshippers seeking health and wealth, they have transformed the expressway into an urban spiritual centre.

item.title: SIR exercise: Citizenship test must be a balancing act
item.description: Beyond documentation, inclusive voting is based on the relationship between citizenship, evidence and democratic participation.
item.content:encoded:
A passport is the most recognisable document the Indian state issues to its citizens. It carries the national emblem, is issued by a sovereign government, and allows its holder to cross international borders as an Indian national.

Yet, during the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, the Ministry of External Affairs clarified that an Indian passport should be understood primarily as a travel document rather than as conclusive proof of citizenship, a distinction that took on particular significance amid the SIR debate.

It is correctly established as a matter of law that a passport is not conclusive proof of citizenship. It is a travel document, issued under the Passports Act, 1967, a statute that itself permits passports to be issued to non-citizens in specified circumstances.

If a passport does not settle the question, what should an ordinary citizen produce when the state asks whether he/she may vote? The question reaches well beyond documentation. It goes to the relationship between citizenship, evidence and democratic participation.

The state government has sought a report from the hospital on the infant deaths.

The authorities are also conducting inspections at other hospitals and nursing homes in the district, where many of the children were treated before being referred to the government facility, The Times of India reported.

Of the 10 newborns who died on Monday, eight were born at other hospitals or nursing homes in the district and were brought to the government medical college in critical condition, The Indian Express quoted hospital Superintendent Prosenjit Bar as saying.

Of the 60 deaths reported till Monday, 44 babies were born elsewhere and later referred to the hospital, the newspaper quoted unidentified state health department officials as saying.

item.title: India to buy Javelin anti-tank missiles from US, says envoy
item.description: The deal would open the door to co-production opportunities, United States Ambassador Sergio Gor said.
item.content:encoded:
India plans to buy Javelin anti-tank guided missile systems from the United States, US Ambassador Sergio Gor said on Friday.

In a post on social media, Gor said the purchase was a “great step forward” in the US-India defence relationship and opened the door to co-production opportunities. “The engagement between our two nations is at record high levels,” he wrote.

New Delhi is yet to comment on Gor’s announcement.

The Javelin is a portable anti-tank missile that can be carried and operated by a single soldier. It uses a “fire-and-forget” system, allowing the missile to track and hit its target without further guidance from the operator.

The weapons system is used by the US military, its partners in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and some other countries such as Ukraine and Saudi Arabia.

The potential Javelin deal comes amid deepening defence relations between the two countries.

In October, India and the US signed a 10-year framework for “major defence partnership”.

The US had designated India as its “major defence partner” in 2016. In 2018, India was elevated to tier one of the Strategic Trade Authorisation, which allows New Delhi to receive license-free access to a range of US military and dual-use technologies.
